title.en: Explain hash function and hash table
Store and search elements with the remainder method

say.en: In a hostel, room numbers tell you exactly where a student lives. You walk straight to room 204; you do not knock on every door. Hashing gives every element such an address. In this lesson: Explain hash function and hash table.
Store and search elements with the remainder method.
Explain collisions.

body.en: Hashing finds an element with a single comparison. A *hash function* computes, from the element itself, the index at which it is stored. A common one is the remainder method: h(element) = element % size of the hash table. The hash table is a list in which each element is stored at the index its hash value gives. To search, compute the hash value of the key and compare the key with the element at that index: one comparison, whatever the size of the list.

title.en: On the board: Building a hash table of size 10

say.en: An empty hash table with ten slots, numbered 0 to 9.
Insert 34: 34 mod 10 is 4, so 34 goes to slot 4. 16 goes to slot 6, and 2 to slot 2.
Insert 93 into slot 3, 80 into slot 0, 77 into slot 7 and 51 into slot 1.
To search 77, compute 77 mod 10, which is 7, and look only in slot 7. One comparison, found.
Now insert 44. 44 mod 10 is 4, but 34 is already there. Two elements, one slot: a collision.

body.en: A collision happens when two or more different elements give the same hash value, for example 34 and 44 with h(x) = x % 10. The second element cannot go into the occupied slot, so a collision resolution technique must decide where it goes. A hash function that maps every element of the list to a unique index is called a perfect hash function; with it, every *search* takes exactly one comparison.

points.en: Collision: h(a) = h(b) for a ≠ b
